opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the most exciting framings right now. When you build an agent and put it in front of real users or a real environment, you get a constant stream of signals: did the task succeed, did the user accept the answer, did the code compile, did the tests pass. Historically a lot of that feedback was just thrown away, or at best someone looked at logs and manually tweaked a prompt. Reinforcement learning gives you a principled way to close that loop, so the agent actually gets better from its own experience instead of staying frozen at whatever the base model shipped with.

The way I think about it, there are a few layers. The first is the reward itself. For a lot of agentic tasks, you can define verifiable rewards. In coding you can run the tests, in math you can check the answer, in data extraction you can compare against a schema. That's where RL has been really successful recently, because the signal is clean and you can't easily game it. Then there are softer signals, like human preferences or an LLM-as-judge score. Those are noisier, and you have to be careful about reward hacking, but they let you extend RL to domains where there's no single right answer.

The second layer is the environment. People underestimate this, but if you want to do RL for agents, you need an environment where the agent can actually take actions, call tools, see results, and do multi-step rollouts. Building good, realistic environments is a big part of the work, and I think it's going to be a big part of how companies differentiate. Your environment and your reward functions encode what you actually care about in your domain.

The third layer is accessibility. For a long time RL felt like something only the big labs could do, because the infrastructure was complicated and expensive. What's changed is that with smaller open models, techniques like GRPO, and better tooling, a team with a specific use case can now take a model, define a reward, and fine-tune it to be really good at their task, often beating much larger general models on that narrow problem. That's a big shift.

So I see RL less as a research curiosity and more as the natural way to turn feedback into improvement. Prompting gets you started, supervised fine-tuning gets you a good baseline from examples, but RL is how you let the agent learn from outcomes. And outcomes are ultimately what you care about.

r001.rationale: The response describes RL as using outcomes to improve and fine-tune an agent, but does not clearly distinguish baking feedback into the model from incorporating feedback interactively at runtime.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I frame it is that reinforcement learning is really the most natural way to turn feedback into behavior, because feedback in the real world almost never comes as a clean label. When you're training an agent, you don't have someone sitting there saying "this token was right, this token was wrong." What you have is an outcome. The task got done or it didn't. The code passed the tests or it didn't. The user came back or they churned. That's a signal, but it's delayed and it's noisy, and it only tells you something about the whole trajectory, not about any individual step. And that's exactly the problem RL was built to solve: how do you take a sparse, outcome-level reward and figure out which of the many decisions the agent made along the way actually caused it.

So for agents specifically, I think of it as closing the loop. Supervised fine-tuning gets you to a point where the model behaves roughly like your demonstrations, but demonstrations are static. They don't tell the model what happens when it deviates. RL lets the agent actually act, make mistakes, and then get corrected on the consequences of those mistakes. That's the piece that was missing. An agent that only ever learned from imitation has never seen its own failure modes, and that's a real problem when it's operating over ten, twenty, fifty steps with tools in the loop.

Now, where it gets interesting, and where a lot of my thinking has gone, is the question of where the feedback comes from. The easy case is when you have a verifiable reward, like math or code with unit tests. That's great because the signal is cheap and it's honest, the model can't really game it. But most of the tasks people actually want agents for aren't like that. They're fuzzy. Was this a good research summary? Did the agent navigate the website well? There you're either using human feedback, which is expensive and inconsistent, or you're using a model as the judge, which is scalable but introduces this whole reward hacking dynamic where the policy learns to exploit whatever quirks the judge has.

So in practice I think the craft of it is less about the RL algorithm and more about reward design and data. The algorithm matters, but honestly the thing that determines whether this works is whether you've built an environment where the feedback actually reflects what you care about, and whether you've got enough diversity in the tasks that the agent generalizes instead of just memorizing a few paths to high reward. That's the unglamorous part, and it's where most of the work is.

r001.rationale: The response describes using feedback from an agent’s actions and outcomes to train behavior, but does not distinguish that from incorporating feedback interactively at runtime.

astra-6.text:
I think reinforcement learning is a natural way to think about incorporating feedback, because an agent is making decisions, taking actions, and observing what happens. The question is: how do you use those outcomes to improve the decisions it makes next time?

The tricky part is defining the feedback. If a user says, “That was helpful,” that’s a useful signal, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you which action was responsible. An agent might have taken several steps, and some of those steps may have been unnecessary or even counterproductive. So you have both a reward-design problem and a credit-assignment problem.

I’d also distinguish between using feedback in the agent’s context and actually updating its policy. You can tell an agent what went wrong and have it try again without changing the model’s weights. Reinforcement learning gives you a way to turn that experience into a more persistent change in behavior. Whether you need that depends on the task, how much feedback you can collect, and how reliably you can measure success.

r001.rationale: It contrasts giving feedback in the agent’s context so it can try again without changing model weights with using reinforcement learning to make a more persistent change in behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reinforcement learning is a natural way to think about feedback when an agent is taking a sequence of actions. You don’t necessarily know whether each individual action was good, but you can observe whether the agent ultimately accomplished the task. Reinforcement learning gives you a framework for using that outcome to improve the policy—the way the agent decides what to do next.

The hard part is defining the reward. If a user gives a thumbs-up or a thumbs-down, that’s useful, but it’s a pretty sparse signal. If the agent took ten steps, which of those steps contributed to the result? And does the feedback reflect correctness, or just whether the answer sounded convincing? You want to be careful that you’re reinforcing the behavior you actually care about.

I’d also distinguish between giving an agent feedback in its context and actually training it from that feedback. An agent can use a correction to do better on its next attempt without updating its weights. Reinforcement learning is a way to make those improvements persist across tasks. So I see it as an important part of the picture, but it depends on having meaningful feedback and a reliable way to measure success.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes runtime feedback, where an agent uses a correction on its next attempt without updating weights, from reinforcement learning that trains persistent improvements across tasks.
